rules.title: It renews on its own
rules.plain: You'll keep getting charged every period until you actively cancel. Set a reminder if you only want it for a while.
rules.ask: When exactly does it renew, and how do I turn auto-renew off?

rules.title: You have to cancel early
rules.plain: Cancelling isn't instant — you must give notice a set number of days before renewal, or you're charged for another round.
rules.ask: How many days' notice do I need to cancel, and how do I give it (online, email, in writing)?

rules.title: You can cancel anytime
rules.plain: No lock-in: you can stop whenever you want (usually it ends at the close of the current billing period).

rules.title: They can raise the price
rules.plain: The price isn't locked. They're allowed to change what you pay, sometimes with only a short notice.
rules.ask: Is my price locked in? How much notice do I get before an increase, and can I cancel without penalty if it goes up?

rules.title: No refunds
rules.plain: Once you pay, you're unlikely to get money back — even if you cancel partway through.
rules.ask: If I cancel early or I'm unhappy, do I get any of my money back?

rules.title: There's a refund path
rules.plain: The terms mention refunds, a money-back guarantee, or a cooling-off period. Check the conditions and deadline.

rules.title: It costs money to leave
rules.plain: Ending the contract early triggers a fee or makes you pay out the rest of the term.
rules.ask: What exactly would I owe if I end this early?

rules.title: Free trial turns into paid
rules.plain: When the trial ends you're switched to a paid plan automatically unless you cancel before it finishes.
rules.ask: What day does the trial end, and will I get a reminder before I'm charged?

rules.title: Extra fees may apply
rules.plain: Beyond the headline price, there can be service, processing, admin, late or other fees. Budget for the real total.
rules.ask: What's the full price with every fee and tax included?

rules.title: They keep your card on file
rules.plain: You're giving them permission to charge your payment method again in the future without asking each time.

rules.title: You can't take them to court
rules.plain: Disputes go to a private arbitrator instead of a judge. It's usually faster but more favorable to companies, and you can't appeal much.
rules.ask: Can I opt out of arbitration, and how?

rules.title: No joining a class action
rules.plain: If they wrong lots of people, you can't team up with them in a group lawsuit — you'd have to go it alone.

rules.title: You give up a jury trial
rules.plain: Even if a case does go to court, you agree a judge alone decides it.

rules.title: You can opt out of arbitration
rules.plain: There's a window (often 30 days) to opt out of forced arbitration. Do it early if you want to keep your right to sue.

rules.title: Small claims court is allowed
rules.plain: You can still bring small disputes to small claims court — cheap and you don't need a lawyer.

rules.title: Your legal consumer rights still apply
rules.plain: The terms admit they can't override consumer protection laws where you live.

rules.title: They can change the rules anytime
rules.plain: They can rewrite these terms later, and simply continuing to use the service counts as agreeing to the new version.
rules.ask: How will I be told about changes, and can I leave without penalty if I don't agree?

rules.title: You'll be warned before changes
rules.plain: They commit to notifying you ahead of time before important changes kick in.
patterns: (notify|notice to|tell|inform) you (in advance|before|at least \d+ days|prior to)

rules.title: They can shut your account
rules.plain: They can suspend or close your account on their own call, sometimes without warning — and you may lose what's in it.

rules.title: Their responsibility is capped
rules.plain: If something goes wrong, the most they'll pay you is limited — often just what you paid them, or a small fixed amount.

rules.title: You cover their legal costs
rules.plain: If someone sues them because of something you did, you agree to pay their legal bills and damages.
rules.ask: What situations would make me responsible for their legal costs?

rules.title: No promises it works
rules.plain: The product is provided 'as is' — they don't guarantee it'll be reliable, accurate, or available.

rules.title: Disputes happen on their turf
rules.plain: The contract picks which country or state's laws apply and where cases are heard — which may be far from you.
patterns: governed by (and construed in accordance with )?the laws? of

rules.title: Your data gets shared
rules.plain: Your personal information can be shared with or sold to other companies like partners, affiliates or advertisers.
rules.ask: Who exactly gets my data, and can I opt out of sharing or selling it?

rules.title: You're tracked for ads
rules.plain: They use cookies or similar tech to follow what you do and show you targeted ads.

rules.title: They can use your stuff
rules.plain: Anything you upload or post, they get a broad (often worldwide, free, forever) right to use, copy and share it.
rules.ask: What can they do with the content I upload, and does that stop if I delete it?

rules.title: Your data may train their AI
rules.plain: What you share might be used to build or improve their algorithms or AI models.

rules.title: They may look at your activity
rules.plain: They reserve the right to monitor, record or review your messages, calls or content.

rules.title: They keep your data
rules.plain: Your information can be kept for a while — even after you close your account.

rules.title: You can get or delete your data
rules.plain: You have the right to access, download, correct or delete your information.

rules.title: Expect marketing messages
rules.plain: By agreeing you may be signing up for promotional emails, texts or calls. Look for an unsubscribe option.

rules.title: You're locked in
rules.plain: There's a minimum period you must stay (and pay) for, even if you want out earlier.
rules.ask: What's the minimum commitment, and what happens if I need to leave before it ends?

rules.title: You're personally on the hook
rules.plain: You personally guarantee the payments — your own money is at risk, not just a business's.

rules.title: It limits what you can do next
rules.plain: There are restrictions on working for competitors, starting a similar business, or poaching clients/staff.
rules.ask: How long and how wide are the non-compete or non-solicit restrictions?
patterns: shall not (directly or indirectly )?(compete|solicit|engage in any business)

rules.title: They can hand the contract to someone else
rules.plain: They may transfer this agreement to another company (e.g. if they're bought) — you might not be able to do the same.

rules.title: Money held as a deposit
rules.plain: There's a deposit or security amount. Check exactly when and how you get it back.
rules.ask: Under what conditions is the deposit returned, and how quickly?

rules.title: There's an age requirement
rules.plain: You must be a certain age (or have a parent's permission) to use this.
patterns: (at least|must be|over|under) (the age of )?(13|16|18|21|thirteen|sixteen|eighteen)( years)?( of age| old)?

jargon.meaning: A private referee settles disputes instead of a court. Usually binding, with little room to appeal.

The specific state or country whose laws apply to the contract.

A lawsuit where many affected people sue together.
Forever. It doesn't expire.

Transfer the contract or rights to someone else.
End the agreement.

Anyone who isn't you or them — partners, vendors, advertisers.
Companies related to them, like parent companies or sister brands.

"Despite" — this part wins even if another part says otherwise.

"According to" or "under".
"Instead of".
Split proportionally — e.g. only paying for the days you used.
Each person can be made to pay the whole amount, not just their share.

Only what's written here counts — verbal promises don't.
Copies signed separately still form one valid contract.
Money held by a neutral party until conditions are met.
A legal claim on your property until a debt is paid.
A formal promise to do (or not do) something.
